prompt: A test for a rare disease is 95% accurate, yet most people who test positive are healthy.
why: When almost nobody has the disease, the 5% of healthy people who test wrong outnumber the few true cases. The base rate decides what a positive means.
trap: The test isn't bad; the disease is rare.

prompt: Someone shy who loves books is assumed to be a librarian, though salespeople vastly outnumber librarians.
why: Even if shy book lovers are likelier to be librarians, there are so many more salespeople that most shy book lovers are salespeople. That's the base rate.
trap: It isn't about who was surveyed.

prompt: A fraud alarm flags 1% of transactions, but real fraud is only 0.01%, so most alerts are false.
why: The alarm fires on 1% of transactions but fraud is only 0.01%, so at most 1 alert in 100 can be real. A tiny base rate makes false alarms the norm.
trap: The alerts aren't outliers; fraud is just rare.

prompt: Before judging a new startup's chances, an investor asks how many startups like it usually succeed.
tells: how many startups like it usually succeed
why: Asking how often startups like this usually succeed starts from the typical rate before the details of this one. That starting point is the base rate.
trap: Not about a biased sample of startups.

prompt: Most car crashes happen near home, mostly because most driving happens near home.
tells: because most driving happens near home
why: Most driving happens near home, so most crashes do too, even if it isn't more dangerous there. More exposure means more events: a base-rate effect.
trap: Home isn't a hidden cause of both.

prompt: An airport scanner alarm sounds, and the guard remembers that almost no travelers carry weapons.
why: Real weapons are so rare that most alarms are false, even from a good scanner. Remembering how rare the thing is means using the base rate.
